```{r setup}
library(knapsack)
suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
median_elapsed <- function(expr, repetitions = 3L, iterations = 1L) {
  expression <- substitute(expr)
  environment <- parent.frame()
  times <- replicate(repetitions, {
    system.time(
      for (i in seq_len(iterations)) eval(expression, envir = environment)
    )[["elapsed"]] / iterations
  })
  median(times)
}
```

The package solves the 0/1 knapsack problem: choose a subset of items whose
total weight is at most `W` and whose total value is as large as possible.
Each function returns the total `value` and the selected row indices in
`elements`.

## Brute-force search

Brute force checks every subset, so its time complexity is O(2^n). It is exact
and useful for small inputs and for checking the other algorithms.

```{r}
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
```

**Question: How long does the algorithm take for n = 16 items?**

The following elapsed time is the median of three runs on the machine that
builds this vignette. It varies by processor and R version. Doubling the number
of items roughly doubles the work because the number of subsets doubles for
each added item.

```{r}
brute_16_time <- median_elapsed(
  brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500)
)
data.frame(items = 16, elapsed_seconds = brute_16_time)
```

## Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming is exact when weights and capacity are integers. It has
O(n W) time complexity, where `n` is the number of items and `W` is the
capacity. The solver updates the value states for all affected capacities at
once and keeps a logical table for reconstructing the selected items.

```{r}
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
```

**Question: How long does the algorithm take for n = 500 items?**

```{r}
dynamic_500_time <- median_elapsed(
  knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500),
  iterations = 20L
)
data.frame(items = 500, capacity = 3500,
           elapsed_seconds = dynamic_500_time)
```

## Greedy heuristic

The greedy solver orders feasible items by value per unit weight and takes the
feasible prefix. It compares that prefix with the best feasible single item,
which gives a 1/2 approximation guarantee for the 0/1 problem. Sorting
dominates its O(n log n) running time.

```{r}
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
```

**Question: How long does the algorithm take for n = 1,000,000 items?**

```{r}
set.seed(42)
large_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = 1e6, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = 1e6, 0, 10000)
)
greedy_1m_time <- median_elapsed(
  greedy_knapsack(x = large_objects, W = 3500)
)
data.frame(items = nrow(large_objects), elapsed_seconds = greedy_1m_time)
```

## Profiling and optimization

We used `profvis` to profile a nested-loop dynamic-programming reference. The
profile showed the capacity loop as the bottleneck: for each item it performs
thousands of interpreted R iterations. The optimized solver updates the
capacity range with vectorized operations instead. It stores one numeric value
vector instead of a full numeric dynamic-programming table, and a logical
decision table for reconstructing the solution. For n = 500 and W = 3,500,
this reduces value-state storage from about 14 MB to about 28 KB; the logical
backtracking table uses about 1.7 MB.

On our Windows 11 machine with R 4.6.0, the median nested-loop reference time
was 0.68 seconds and the optimized solver took about 0.006 seconds per call
(roughly 113 times faster in this run). The required-size timings on that
machine were about 0.14 seconds for brute force with n = 16, 0.008 seconds for
dynamic programming with n = 500 and W = 3,500, and 0.03 seconds for greedy
search with n = 1,000,000. These short timings are machine-specific; the chunks
recalculate them when the vignette is built.

The benchmark below compares the vectorized implementation with a simple
nested-loop reference. The reported speedup is machine-specific and is
calculated from the timings printed by this run.

```{r}
dynamic_loop_reference <- function(x, W) {
  n <- nrow(x)
  table <- matrix(0, nrow = n + 1L, ncol = W + 1L)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    table[i + 1L, ] <- table[i, ]
    if (x$w[[i]] <= W) {
      for (capacity in seq.int(x$w[[i]], W)) {
        table[i + 1L, capacity + 1L] <- max(
          table[i, capacity + 1L],
          table[i, capacity - x$w[[i]] + 1L] + x$v[[i]]
        )
      }
    }
  }
  table[n + 1L, W + 1L]
}

reference_value <- dynamic_loop_reference(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], 3500)
optimized_result <- knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], 3500)
reference_time <- median_elapsed(
  dynamic_loop_reference(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], 3500)
)
optimized_time <- median_elapsed(
  knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], 3500), iterations = 20L
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(reference_value, optimized_result$value)))
data.frame(reference_seconds = reference_time,
           optimized_seconds = optimized_time,
           speedup = reference_time / optimized_time)
```

To reproduce the profile interactively in RStudio, run this chunk with
`eval = TRUE` after installing `profvis`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
profvis::profvis({
  dynamic_loop_reference(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500)
})
profvis::profvis({
  for (i in seq_len(20L)) {
    knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500)
  }
})
```

## Parallel brute-force search

The starred parallelization exercise is implemented by the optional
`parallel` argument. It divides subset ranges among detected CPU cores and
uses socket workers, so the same implementation works on Windows, macOS, and
Linux. The sequential version remains the default because starting workers can
cost more than searching a small number of subsets.

```{r}
parallel_objects <- knapsack_objects[1:18, ]
sequential_result <- brute_force_knapsack(parallel_objects, W = 3500)
parallel_result <- brute_force_knapsack(
  parallel_objects, W = 3500, parallel = TRUE
)
sequential_time <- median_elapsed(
  brute_force_knapsack(parallel_objects, W = 3500)
)
parallel_time <- median_elapsed(
  brute_force_knapsack(parallel_objects, W = 3500, parallel = TRUE)
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sequential_result, parallel_result)))
data.frame(items = 18, sequential_seconds = sequential_time,
           parallel_seconds = parallel_time,
           speedup = sequential_time / parallel_time)
```

Parallel speedup depends on physical core count and worker startup overhead.
For small n, parallel execution can be slower; increasing n makes the
independent subset ranges large enough to offset that overhead. On our Windows
11 machine with 8 physical cores, n = 18 took a median 0.57 seconds
sequentially and 0.25 seconds in parallel (about 2.3 times faster). GitHub
Actions limits parallel checks to at most two cores, so its measured speedup
can differ.
